# ALife

Spatial artificial life: grid cellular automata (life-like, cyclic and Wolfram's elementary rules), continuous systems (reaction-diffusion, Turing patterns, Lenia), agent populations (boids, Physarum, diffusion-limited aggregation) and structural growth (L-systems, space colonization), plus the measurement layer every one of them makes its claims through.

18 source file(s), 968 public symbol(s), 881 of them carrying KDoc. Everything below is the documentation that lives beside the code — the same text the [completion documentation panel](../completion_doc_browser.md) shows in the editor. ## alife.kt { #alife-kt }

Spatial artificial life for the Field stdlib — the *continuous / grid / agent* half of ALife, the
counterpart to the graph-rewriting half already here (`growing.kt`, `dynamic_graph_systems.kt`,
`interactionnets.kt`, `booleannetworks.kt`) and to the constraint-based generator in `wfc.kt`.

Six files:

- **`alife.kt`** (this one) — the substrate: [`IntGrid`](alife.md#alife-kt-intgrid), the grid↔[`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img) bridges, and the
  **measurement** layer. Everything else in the family makes its claims through the functions at
  the bottom of this file.
- **`alife_ca.kt`** — discrete cellular automata: [`LifeRule`](alife.md#alife-ca-kt-liferule) parsed from `B3/S23`, outer-totalistic
  and cyclic multi-state CA, Wolfram's elementary 1-D rules rendered as a space-time [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img), and a
  3-D life-like CA that marches out to a [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh).
- **`alife_continuous.kt`** — Gray–Scott reaction–diffusion, Turing patterns, and Lenia
  (continuous CA: ring-kernel convolution plus a growth mapping).
- **`alife_field.kt`** — the inline `ToHTML` views for [`IntGrid`](alife.md#alife-kt-intgrid), `GrayScottState` and `LeniaRun`,
  kept separate so the five system files name nothing from Field's visualizer.
- **`alife_agents.kt`** — boids flocking, a Physarum/slime-mould deposit–sense–move population over
  a trail [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img), and diffusion-limited aggregation.
- **`alife_lsystem.kt`** — a bracketed/parametric L-system with a turtle that emits
  [`afield.geometry.path.FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline)s, and space-colonization branching.

Design choices, all deliberate:

- **Built on [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img), not on a private raster.** Every continuous system is an `Img -> Img` step, so a
  reaction–diffusion field pipelines straight into `gaussianBlur`, `colormap`, `connectedComponents`,
  `isoContourFLines` and `asHeightSdf` with no glue. Nothing here reimplements convolution.
- **A step is a value, not a side effect.** `step()` returns the next state; you keep the frames you
  want. The one exception is the mutable agent populations, where copying 50 000
  agents per frame would be the whole cost.
- **Deterministic from a seed.** Every stochastic system takes a `seed: Long` and uses its own
  `kotlin.random.Random`, so a figure in the docs is reproducible and a regression is a diff.
- **No external dependency.** Pure Kotlin over `FloatArray`/`IntArray`.
- **Measured, not asserted.** The functions under "Measurement" exist because "it produced pixels"
  is not evidence. A flock is a population whose [`polarization`](alife.md#alife-kt--polarization) is high *and* whose
  [`nearestNeighborDistances`](alife.md#alife-kt--nearestneighbordistances) have a floor; a DLA cluster is one whose [`massRadiusDimension`](alife.md#alife-kt--massradiusdimension) is
  ~1.7; a Gray–Scott spot regime is one whose [`blobShapes`](alife.md#alife-kt--blobshapes) are round. Each of those is a number a
  control arm gets wrong.

Out of scope: GPU implementations (that is Field 4 / StackSL / RectSL — these are
CPU reference implementations you can read), and any system needing a trained model.

## alife_agents.kt { #alife-agents-kt }

Agent-based spatial ALife: boids flocking, a Physarum (slime-mould) deposit–sense–move population
over a trail [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img), and diffusion-limited aggregation.

See `alife.kt` for the family overview.

These are the three canonical demonstrations that **global order can have no global rule**: a flock's
alignment, a slime mould's transport network and a dendrite's fractal dimension are all properties
nothing in the code mentions. Which is exactly why each one here ships with a control arm — a run of
the same code with one interaction switched off — because "emergence" is otherwise the easiest thing
in computing to claim and the hardest to check. See [`polarization`](alife.md#alife-kt--polarization), [`Img.topShare`](alife.md#alife-kt--topshare) and
[`massRadiusDimension`](alife.md#alife-kt--massradiusdimension) for the three numbers those controls fail.

Unlike the rest of the family these types are **mutable**: `step()` advances the population in place.
Copying 50 000 agents per frame would be the entire cost of a Physarum run, and the systems are
simulations rather than values.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/agents/alife_agents.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/agents/alife_agents/)

**Used in:** [Spatial artificial life](../alife_examples.md)

## alife_animate.kt { #alife-animate-kt }

One shared way to *animate* the `alife*.kt` family — because every system in it is a time
evolution, and a montage of frozen generations is the one view that hides the thing they are about.

The whole file is [`Box.animateEvolution`](alife.md#alife-animate-kt--animateevolution) plus four small "show a prefix of something" helpers. It sits
apart from the five simulation files for the same reason `alife_field.kt` does: those files name nothing
from Field's box runtime, and this one is entirely about it ([`Box`](workspace.md#boxes-kt-box), [`Frames`](workspace.md#phased-kt-frames), `display`).

**Pacing is the craft, and it is the reason this is a shared helper rather than a copied loop.** The
naive animation — one simulation step per displayed frame — is wrong for almost every system here, and
wrong in two opposite directions:

 - Gray–Scott needs about **6000** explicit-Euler steps to reach its named regime. One step per frame at
   20 fps is five minutes of a clip in which nothing happens.
 - Conway's glider moves one cell per **four** generations. Forty steps per frame is a strobe.

So [`Box.animateEvolution`](alife.md#alife-animate-kt--animateevolution) takes the *whole* evolution — `totalSteps` — and the `seconds` it should occupy,
and derives the steps per displayed frame. Live playback uses monotonic time. Frame-synchronous recording
installs an [`AnimationClock`](workspace.md#runloop-kt-animationclock) whose time is exactly `frameIndex / fps`, so the same seed produces the same
ordered simulation states even when browser painting or encoding is slow. Capture performance changes how
long the build takes, never which states enter the movie.

**A linear step schedule is not a neutral choice, and for some of these systems it is the wrong one.**
Reaction–diffusion and Lenia are *log-time* processes: the visible change from step 60 to step 600 is
about the same as from step 600 to step 6000. Spend equal steps on equal wall-clock and the clip
front-loads — measured as the mean absolute luma difference between the extracted frames of the
Gray–Scott clip on `alife_examples.md`, a linear schedule gave **42.09** from the first frame to the
middle and **3.98** from the middle to the last: the reader watches it finish and then waits. So
[`Box.animateEvolution`](alife.md#alife-animate-kt--animateevolution) takes a `ramp`, and the schedule it drives is geometric rather than linear. See
that parameter for the arithmetic.

**The step counter belongs in the frame.** Every call site here labels its panels with the step number,
which is not decoration: it is how "did this clip actually reach the regime?" is answered by *looking* at
the last frame of the recorded mp4 rather than by trusting the schedule. A clip whose final label reads
`step 2100 / 6000` is a failed clip, and it says so on its face.

**The range policy from `alife_field.kt` applies with more force here, not less.** A colour map whose
range is taken from the frame makes an animation of a growing structure appear to stand still, and makes
a saturating field indistinguishable from a dying one. So every call site passes explicit `lo`/`hi` to
[`Img.colormap`](imaging.md#imaging-field-kt--colormap). Auto-ranging is a per-figure mistake and a per-*frame* lie.

## alife_bml.kt { #alife-bml-kt }

The Biham–Middleton–Levine traffic model on the GPU: a torus of cells, each empty or holding one
car, advanced by a single full-screen fragment pass into a ping-pong texture.

### The rule

There are two kinds of car. Eastbound cars (red) only ever move one cell to the right, southbound
cars (blue) only ever move one cell down, and the two take turns: on even steps every eastbound
car whose right-hand cell is empty moves into it, all at once; on odd steps the southbound cars do
the same downwards. The grid wraps in both directions. Nothing else happens, and no car is ever
created or destroyed.

What makes the model famous is that its only parameter, the fraction of cells holding a car, has
a sharp transition: at low density the cars sort themselves into diagonal bands that flow freely,
at high density a single jam spanning the grid forms and nothing moves. On a 512 × 512 torus, 0.20
reaches a moving fraction of 0.998 and 0.45 reaches 0 by step 1750, while 0.32 is near the
transition and decays slowly from flow toward a jam.

### One texel is one cell

[`ShaderBmlSystem`](alife.md#alife-bml-kt-shaderbmlsystem) holds the state in an RGBA8 ping-pong target: red at 1 is an eastbound car, blue
at 1 a southbound one, black an empty cell. Each frame the pass reads the previous frame's texture
and writes this one, so one frame is one half-step, and a full step (both colours) takes two
frames. An 8-bit target is enough because the values are only ever 0 or 1.

The update is a pure gather. A cell becomes empty if it holds a car of the moving colour and the
cell ahead is empty, becomes that car if it is empty and the cell behind holds one, and otherwise
keeps what it had. Each cell decides from three texels of the previous frame, so the whole grid
advances in parallel with no conflicts and conserves the car count exactly.

The first frame after construction or [`ShaderBmlSystem.reset`](alife.md#alife-bml-kt--shaderbmlsystem--reset) ignores the previous texture and
scatters cars instead, each cell independently holding a car with probability
[`ShaderBmlSettings.density`](alife.md#alife-bml-kt--shaderbmlsettings--density), eastbound with probability [`ShaderBmlSettings.eastboundFraction`](alife.md#alife-bml-kt--shaderbmlsettings--eastboundfraction).

### Getting one on screen

`installInto` registers the simulation as a pre-target of the render list and blits it to the
window. As with [`ShaderDlaSystem`](alife.md#alife-dla-kt-shaderdlasystem), constructing it inside a box seeds that box's `fragment` tab with
the update rule, so the rule arrives as source you can edit. The CPU-side alife family does not
have this model; nothing here reads the grid back.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/agents/alife_bml.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/agents/alife_bml/)

## alife_continuous.kt { #alife-continuous-kt }

Continuous spatial ALife: reaction–diffusion (Gray–Scott / Turing) and Lenia, all shaped as
`Img -> Img` steps so they compose with the imaging family.

See `alife.kt` for the family overview.

Every system here is a **field**, not a lattice of labels, so the measurements that matter are
different from the discrete half: not "is this pattern periodic" but "what shape are its features"
([`Img.blobShapes`](alife.md#alife-kt--blobshapes)) and "what length scale did it choose" ([`Img.correlationLength`](alife.md#alife-kt--correlationlength)). The one exception,
and the reason the two halves live in the same family, is [`leniaFromLifeRule`](alife.md#alife-continuous-kt--leniafromliferule): Lenia in its discrete
limit *is* a life-like CA, and that gives this file's float convolution and `alife_ca.kt`'s integer
neighbour counting a claim they must agree on exactly.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/agents/alife_continuous.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/agents/alife_continuous/)

**Used in:** [Spatial artificial life](../alife_examples.md)

Body in `alife_field.kt` ([`alifeLeniaRunHtml`](alife.md#alife-field-kt--alifeleniarunhtml)). A saturated field is constant at 1 and an auto-ranged colour map draws it black, i.e. identical to death — so this view is the one place in the family where the range policy changes the result rather than tidying it. |

## alife_dla.kt { #alife-dla-kt }

Diffusion-limited aggregation on the GPU: a buffer of random walkers stepped, stuck and drawn by a
single vertex shader, with the growing cluster held in a texture rather than in any Kotlin data
structure.

The CPU version of the same process is [`dlaCluster`](alife.md#alife-agents-kt--dlacluster) in `alife_agents.kt`, and the two answer
different questions. `dlaCluster` returns points you can measure, with [`massRadiusDimension`](alife.md#alife-kt--massradiusdimension) and a
control arm to measure them against. What is here returns an image, at a walker count the CPU
version cannot reach, and nothing reads it back. Measure DLA with `alife_agents.kt`; watch one grow
at window resolution with this.

### The state is three channels of one texture

[`ShaderDlaSystem`](alife.md#alife-dla-kt-shaderdlasystem) renders into a single RGBA16F ping-pong target, and every part of the simulation
except the walkers themselves lives in its channels:

- red is solidity, and a pixel counts as part of the cluster once red reaches `solidThreshold`;
- green marks where the walkers are this frame, and nothing carries it forward;
- blue is age, rising while a pixel is solid and falling back when it stops being, which is what a
  colour ramp reads if you want tips to look younger than the interior.

### Two draws per frame, and no compute pass

The target is cleared at the start of every frame, so a full-screen `preserve` pass runs first and
rebuilds the carried state by sampling the *previous* frame's image: red decays, blue grows or
decays, and the seed disc is held solid. The particle pass then draws one additively blended point
per walker. Both read the previous frame rather than the one being built, and they run in the order
they were added to the target.

All of the simulation is in that second pass's *vertex* shader. It reads its walker from an
addressable buffer through a push-constant pointer, probes the four neighbours of its pixel in the
previous frame's red channel, and either sticks where it stands or takes one axis-aligned random
step; then it writes the walker back. Drawing the point and advancing the simulation are the same
draw call.

### A stuck walker lasts one frame

A walker that sticks emits one red splat and is respawned at a uniformly random position on the
next frame, so `particleCount` bounds how many walkers are in flight rather than how large the
cluster can get. The cluster is only ever the red channel, which is also why it is mortal: red
loses `solidDecayPerFrame` every frame whether or not anything is still attaching to it, so at the
defaults a pixel that took one splat and nothing since falls back under the threshold about 500
frames later.

### Getting one on screen

`installInto` registers the simulation as a pre-target of the render list and blits the result to
the window. Constructing the system inside a box also seeds that box's shader properties from the
particle pass, so the walk arrives as source you can edit rather than as a closed component; the
diffusion-limited aggregation section of
[`afield_four_graphics.md`](../afield_four_graphics.md) is the worked version of that, and says why
it carries no figure.

## alife_evolve.kt { #alife-evolve-kt }

The search half of this family: rule sets as **genomes**, the measurements in `alife.kt` as
**fitness**, and `PopulationSearch` as the engine that connects them.

Until this file existed every figure on the ALife page was "run a fixed rule and measure it". The
measuring vocabulary was already here and was already good — `stateEntropyBits`,
`massRadiusDimension`, `blobShapes`, `translationBetween`, `LeniaRun.centroidDrift` — and each of
those is a fitness function with nobody calling it. This file supplies the missing halves: a
[`GenomeOps`](search.md#populationsearch-kt-genomeops) for three families ([`LifeRuleGenome`](alife.md#alife-evolve-kt-liferulegenome), [`LeniaGenome`](alife.md#alife-evolve-kt-leniagenome), [`LSystemGenome`](alife.md#alife-evolve-kt-lsystemgenome)) and an
[`Objective`](search.md#populationsearch-kt-objective) for each, assembled out of statistics that were already in the file next door.

There is **no search code here**. Every driver comes from [`PopulationSearch`](search.md#populationsearch-kt-populationsearch), which is also what
`FunctionEvolve.evolve` runs on. That is the point: one engine, several genomes, rather than a
third private optimizer.

**Every objective in this file evaluates every candidate from the same fixed initial condition.**
A Lenia rule is seeded from `leniaSeed(..., seed = initialSeed)`, a CA rule from the same
[`randomSoup`](alife.md#alife-evolve-kt--randomsoup), an L-system from the same axiom. A search that re-randomised the initial condition
per candidate would be selecting on the luck of the draw, and the resulting "improvement" would be
mostly the search rediscovering that some soups are easier than others. Where robustness across
initial conditions *is* the question, [`caEdgeOfChaosObjective`](alife.md#alife-evolve-kt--caedgeofchaosobjective) takes several soups and reports one
[`Evaluation.cases`](search.md#populationsearch-kt--evaluation--cases) entry each, which is what makes `Selection.LEXICASE` meaningful here.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/agents/alife_evolve.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/agents/alife_evolve/)

**Used in:** [Spatial artificial life](../alife_examples.md), [Agent transcript gallery](../agent_transcripts.md), [Braitenberg vehicles with memory](../braitenberg_vehicles.md)

## alife_field.kt { #alife-field-kt }

Inline `ToHTML` views for the `alife*.kt` family — what a box draws when you *evaluate* an [`IntGrid`](alife.md#alife-kt-intgrid)
or a [`GrayScottState`](alife.md#alife-continuous-kt-grayscottstate), with nothing to set up.

`alife.kt` and `alife_continuous.kt` name only the three entry points here ([`alifeGridHtml`](alife.md#alife-field-kt--alifegridhtml),
[`alifeGrayScottHtml`](alife.md#alife-field-kt--alifegrayscotthtml), [`alifeLeniaRunHtml`](alife.md#alife-field-kt--alifeleniarunhtml)), each from a one-line `toHTML` override, and inherit
every pixel of their view from them.

**The range policy:**

 - **Every scale is named in the caption**, with both endpoints spelled out in the units of the
   thing being shown.
 - **Domains are fixed by meaning, not by the frame.** An [`IntGrid`](alife.md#alife-kt-intgrid)'s states run `0 .. maxState`; a
   Gray–Scott `v` runs `0 .. 1`, the range the reaction is defined on, *not* `min .. max` of this
   particular field. Auto-range a saturated Lenia field — constant at 1 — and it maps to the bottom
   of the ramp: solid black, identical to a field that has died.
 - **One pixel per cell, never resampled.** The `<img>` is scaled by an integer factor with
   `image-rendering:pixelated`, so cell coordinates and pixel coordinates stay the same thing and a
   reader can count. A filtered upscale destroys exactly the local structure a CA is about.
 - **A flat field says so.** If every cell holds the same value the caption reports it, because a
   uniform panel is otherwise indistinguishable from a broken one.

`AlifeGallery`'s `inline-view` figure decodes the base64 PNG back out of the emitted HTML and
asserts the colour of individual pixels against the value the caption claims for them.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/agents/alife_field.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/agents/alife_field/)

## alife_fire.kt { #alife-fire-kt }

Fire spreading through a forest on the GPU: a fixed scatter of trees, fire that you light by
drawing into a texture, and four kinds of fire, one per colour channel, that compete for the same
trees.

### The rule

Each texel is a tree or bare ground, decided once by a hash of its position and
[`ShaderForestFireSettings.randomSeed`](alife.md#alife-fire-kt--shaderforestfiresettings--randomseed), so the forest is the same every run with the same seed. A
tree is *ready*, *burning* or *recovering*, and which it is lives in one number per kind of fire: 1
the frame it catches, then falling by that kind's [`ShaderForestFireSettings.refractoryDecayPerFrame`](alife.md#alife-fire-kt--shaderforestfiresettings--refractorydecayperframe)
each frame. Above [`ShaderForestFireSettings.activeFireThreshold`](alife.md#alife-fire-kt--shaderforestfiresettings--activefirethreshold) it is burning; below
[`ShaderForestFireSettings.readyThreshold`](alife.md#alife-fire-kt--shaderforestfiresettings--readythreshold) it can catch again; in between it is recovering and
cannot. A ready tree catches when a burning neighbour's fire, times
[`ShaderForestFireSettings.spreadGain`](alife.md#alife-fire-kt--shaderforestfiresettings--spreadgain), reaches [`ShaderForestFireSettings.ignitionThreshold`](alife.md#alife-fire-kt--shaderforestfiresettings--ignitionthreshold) and a
random draw against [`ShaderForestFireSettings.spreadProbability`](alife.md#alife-fire-kt--shaderforestfiresettings--spreadprobability) lets it across, or when the
ignition texture at that texel reaches the threshold. If several kinds could take it, the strongest wins, and
catching one kind sets the other three to zero.

Because trees recover, this is an excitable medium rather than a fire that leaves ash: a front
passes, the forest behind it recovers, and a second front can follow the first. A front broken by
bare ground curls at the break, and steady ignition makes a train of rings.

### What is in each texture

[`ShaderForestFireSystem.state`](alife.md#alife-fire-kt--shaderforestfiresystem--state) holds the four fire levels in RGBA; it is what [`imageView`](alife.md#alife-fire-kt--shaderforestfiresystem--imageview) returns.
[`ShaderForestFireSystem.fireInput`](alife.md#alife-fire-kt--shaderforestfiresystem--fireinput) is where ignition is drawn, RGBA one kind per channel, carried
forward and faded by [`ShaderForestFireSettings.ignitionDecayPerFrame`](alife.md#alife-fire-kt--shaderforestfiresettings--ignitiondecayperframe).
[`ShaderForestFireSystem.ink`](alife.md#alife-fire-kt--shaderforestfiresystem--ink) is a colour that burning trees pass on to their neighbours, so that what
you draw into it travels with the fire. The preview colours each kind red, green, blue or magenta,
tinted by the ink.

### Lighting it

Nothing burns until something is lit. Draw into [`ShaderForestFireSystem.fireInput`](alife.md#alife-fire-kt--shaderforestfiresystem--fireinput) with a module
built on [`ShaderForestFireSystem.fireInputParameters`](alife.md#alife-fire-kt--shaderforestfiresystem--fireinputparameters), which blends additively: a fragment writing
`vec4(1, 0, 0, 0)` lights the red kind there. As with [`ShaderDlaSystem`](alife.md#alife-dla-kt-shaderdlasystem), constructing the system
inside a box seeds that box's `fragment` tab with the spreading rule, so the rule arrives as source
you can edit.

All but the sizes and format are bound as lambdas, so changing one while it runs takes effect on the next frame; changing the forest itself ([`treeDensity`](alife.md#alife-fire-kt--shaderforestfiresettings--treedensity), [`treeScalePx`](alife.md#alife-fire-kt--shaderforestfiresettings--treescalepx), [`treeJitter`](alife.md#alife-fire-kt--shaderforestfiresettings--treejitter), [`randomSeed`](alife.md#alife-fire-kt--shaderforestfiresettings--randomseed)) regrows it in place.

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">ShaderForestFireSystem</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">renderer</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Renderer</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">fromContext</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">configure</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ShaderForestFireSettings</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">Unit</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="p">{</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Target</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">HasImageView</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">HasImageViewArray</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/agents/alife_fire/#L168)

The file overview above describes the rule and the encoding.

## alife_lbm.kt { #alife-lbm-kt }

A two-dimensional fluid on the GPU by the lattice Boltzmann method, with a control texture you draw
obstacles, forces and dye sources into, and a dye field that the flow carries.

### The method

Every texel is a lattice site holding nine numbers, the D2Q9 populations: how much fluid at that
site is moving with each of the nine velocities `(0,0)`, the four axis neighbours and the four
diagonals. A step is two moves. *Collision* relaxes each site's populations a fraction
[`ShaderLatticeBoltzmannSettings.relaxation`](alife.md#alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--relaxation) of the way toward the equilibrium for that site's own
density and velocity (the BGK operator); *streaming* then moves each population one site along its
direction. A population that would stream out of a solid site is reflected back where it came from
instead, which is the no-slip wall. Density and velocity are never stored as such; they are sums
over the nine populations. The viscosity follows from the relaxation, `(1/relaxation - 0.5) / 3` in
lattice units, so values near 2 are runny and turbulent and values near 1 are syrupy.

The method is only accurate while the fluid is slow against the lattice, below about 0.1 sites per
step; [`ShaderLatticeBoltzmannSettings.maxVelocity`](alife.md#alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--maxvelocity) clamps it so that a strong push degrades the
physics rather than the numbers.

### What is in each texture

[`ShaderLatticeBoltzmannSystem.fluid`](alife.md#alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsystem--fluid) holds the populations in three RGBA32F attachments, written by
one pass: attachment 0 holds directions 0–3, attachment 1 directions 4–7, and attachment 2 holds
direction 8 in red, then density, velocity x and velocity y, so attachment 2 is also the readable
velocity field. [`ShaderLatticeBoltzmannSystem.controls`](alife.md#alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsystem--controls) holds, per texel, red obstacle (solid at or
above [`ShaderLatticeBoltzmannSettings.solidThreshold`](alife.md#alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--solidthreshold)), green and blue a velocity to steer toward,
and alpha a dye source. [`ShaderLatticeBoltzmannSystem.dye`](alife.md#alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsystem--dye) is colour advected by the velocity and
fed by the dye source, by speed and by vorticity.

Every frame runs the controls (carried forward, then whatever you have added), then
[`ShaderLatticeBoltzmannSettings.stepsPerFrame`](alife.md#alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--stepsperframe) fluid steps, then the dye.

### Driving it

A fresh system is still water: nothing moves until something pushes. There are two ways. Set
[`ShaderLatticeBoltzmannSettings.baseVelocity`](alife.md#alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--basevelocity) for a wind everywhere, which with
[`ShaderLatticeBoltzmannSettings.wrapX`](alife.md#alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--wrapx) makes a wind tunnel; or draw into the controls texture with
a module built on [`ShaderLatticeBoltzmannSystem.controlsParameters`](alife.md#alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsystem--controlsparameters), which blends additively, so a
fragment that writes `vec4(1, 0, 0, 0)` marks a texel solid and `vec4(0, 0.2, 0, 1)` pushes it right
and releases dye there. The controls texture is carried from frame to frame, so a module that draws
every frame accumulates; [`ShaderLatticeBoltzmannSettings.obstacleDecayPerFrame`](alife.md#alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--obstacledecayperframe) and its siblings let
old marks fade.

As with [`ShaderDlaSystem`](alife.md#alife-dla-kt-shaderdlasystem), constructing it inside a box seeds that box's `fragment` tab with the
collision-and-streaming rule, so the physics arrives as source you can edit.

| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--stepsperframe"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">stepsPerFrame</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Lattice steps per frame. The fluid moves at most a fraction of a site per step, so at one step a frame a flow takes thousands of frames to cross the lattice; this is the speed of the film, not of the physics. The dye is advected once per frame, the whole distance. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--relaxation"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">relaxation</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | The BGK relaxation rate ω, in (0, 2): how far each collision moves the populations toward equilibrium. Viscosity is `(1/ω - 0.5) / 3`, so larger is thinner and less stable. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--basedensity"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">baseDensity</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | The density the fluid starts at and that solid sites are held at. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--basevelocity"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">baseVelocity</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vector2f</span></code> | A wind applied everywhere, in sites per step; the fluid starts moving at this velocity. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--initialnoise"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">initialNoise</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | Random velocity, in sites per step, added to every site when the fluid starts or is cleared. A symmetric setup computed on a GPU stays exactly symmetric, so without it a wake that ought to shed vortices can sit still for ever; the default is small enough not to show. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--driveblend"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">driveBlend</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | How far each site's velocity is pulled toward [`baseVelocity`](alife.md#alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--basevelocity) each step, 0 to 1. This is what keeps the wind blowing against the drag of obstacles, and also what erases a wake: a disturbance fades over about `1 / driveBlend` steps, so small values let wakes travel far. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--controlvelocityscale"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">controlVelocityScale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | Scale from the controls texture's green and blue to a velocity added each step. A push held in place keeps accelerating the fluid there until [`maxVelocity`](alife.md#alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--maxvelocity) stops it. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--maxvelocity"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">maxVelocity</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | The speed no site may exceed, in sites per step. Above about 0.3 the method becomes unstable. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--wrapx"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">wrapX</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code> | Whether the lattice wraps left to right; otherwise the edges clamp. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--wrapy"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">wrapY</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code> | Whether the lattice wraps top to bottom. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--bordersolidpx"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">borderSolidPx</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | A solid frame this many pixels thick around the edge; 0 for none. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--solidthreshold"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">solidThreshold</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | The controls' red value at or above which a site is solid. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--obstacledecayperframe"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">obstacleDecayPerFrame</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | How much each obstacle mark fades per frame. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--directiondecayperframe"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">directionDecayPerFrame</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | How much each steering mark fades per frame, toward zero from either side. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--dyesourcedecayperframe"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">dyeSourceDecayPerFrame</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | How much each dye-source mark fades per frame. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--controldirectionlimit"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">controlDirectionLimit</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | The largest steering value the controls texture keeps, either sign, so accumulated pushes saturate. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--dyedecayperframe"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">dyeDecayPerFrame</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | The fraction of the dye that fades each frame. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--dyeadvectionscale"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">dyeAdvectionScale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | How far, in multiples of the velocity times [`stepsPerFrame`](alife.md#alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--stepsperframe), the dye is carried each frame. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--controldyegain"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">controlDyeGain</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | Dye released per frame by a full dye-source mark. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--speeddyegain"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">speedDyeGain</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | Dye released by speed above the wind. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--curldyegain"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">curlDyeGain</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | Dye released by vorticity, which is what makes vortices draw themselves. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--dyelimit"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">dyeLimit</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | The brightest the dye may get. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--speedvisualizationgain"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">speedVisualizationGain</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | Gain from speed to brightness in the speed and velocity views. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--curlvisualizationgain"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">curlVisualizationGain</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | Gain from vorticity to saturation in the curl view. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--densityvisualizationgain"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">densityVisualizationGain</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | Gain from density deviation to brightness in the density view. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--compositedyeexposure"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">compositeDyeExposure</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | Exposure of the dye in the composite view. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--compositevelocitygain"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">compositeVelocityGain</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | Weight of the velocity colour in the composite view. |
| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--compositecurlgain"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">compositeCurlGain</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span></code> | Weight of the vorticity colour in the composite view. |

### ShaderLatticeBoltzmannSystem { #alife-lbm-kt-shaderlatticeboltzmannsystem }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">ShaderLatticeBoltzmannSystem</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">renderer</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Renderer</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">fromContext</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">configure</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ShaderLatticeBoltzmannSettings</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">Unit</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="p">{</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Target</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">HasImageView</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">HasImageViewArray</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/agents/alife_lbm/#L207)

A D2Q9 lattice Boltzmann fluid: controls, one fluid step and dye advection, each a full-screen pass into its own ping-pong target. Build one, call [`installInto`](alife.md#alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsystem--installinto), then push it, with [`ShaderLatticeBoltzmannSettings.baseVelocity`](alife.md#alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsettings--basevelocity) or a module from [`controlsParameters`](alife.md#alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsystem--controlsparameters). The file overview above describes the method and what each texture holds.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |

| <a id="alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsystem--settings"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">settings</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/agents/alife_lbm/#L214) | The settings this system was built with, after `configure` ran, and the handle for changing it live. |

Draw into it with modules from [`controlsParameters`](alife.md#alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsystem--controlsparameters), registered with [`addControls`](alife.md#alife-lbm-kt--shaderlatticeboltzmannsystem--addcontrols). |

The box adopts this one. |

## alife_lsystem.kt { #alife-lsystem-kt }

Structural spatial ALife: a bracketed, parametric, optionally stochastic L-system with a turtle that
emits [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline)s, plus space-colonization branching.

See `alife.kt` for the family overview.

L-systems are the odd one out in this family and belong in it for a precise reason: they are the one
generative system here whose output can be checked **exactly and combinatorially** rather than
statistically. Lindenmayer's original algae system has Fibonacci-length derivations; the Koch
*snowflake* has exactly `3 * 4^n` forward symbols after `n` rewrites (the quadratic Koch island this
file also ships, [`LSYSTEM_KOCH_QUADRATIC`](alife.md#alife-lsystem-kt--lsystem-koch-quadratic), has `5^n` — check which one you are asserting about); the
Koch snowflake's turtle path closes to a
measurable area. Those are equalities, not distributions, so they are the sharpest evidence in the
whole family — and they exercise the same turtle that draws the pretty trees.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/agents/alife_lsystem.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/agents/alife_lsystem/)

**Used in:** [Spatial artificial life](../alife_examples.md)

## alife_physarum_gpu.kt { #alife-physarum-gpu-kt }

Jones' Physarum on the GPU, built on the [`TrailField`](alife.md#alife-trail-kt-trailfield) stigmergy field in `alife_trail.kt`.

[`ShaderPhysarumSystem`](alife.md#alife-physarum-gpu-kt-shaderphysarumsystem) keeps a million agents (by default) in an addressable buffer and steps
them in one vertex-shader draw per frame: each agent samples the previous frame's trail at three
sensors, turns toward the strongest, steps, writes itself back and deposits one additive point.
Up to four species share the field, one per channel, each attracted by its own trail and repelled
by the others. `sensing = false` is the random-turn control arm, so [`Img.topShare`](alife.md#alife-kt--topshare) of the trail
read back with [`TrailField.read`](alife.md#alife-trail-kt--trailfield--read) separates a network from a random walk, as it does for the CPU
[`PhysarumSwarm`](alife.md#alife-agents-kt-physarumswarm).

Unlike the CPU model there is no one-agent-per-cell exclusion; at about one agent per pixel the
density does that job.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/agents/alife_physarum_gpu.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/agents/alife_physarum_gpu/)

## alife_script.kt { #alife-script-kt }

Per-agent **scripted** behaviour for ALife: a coroutine each agent runs as its own little program,
on a fixed-step virtual clock, composing into weighted steering drives.

See `alife.kt` for the family overview, and `alife_agents.kt` for the family this completes.

### Why this exists

Everything in `alife_agents.kt` is a **global rule**. A flock is `BoidFlock.step(p: BoidParams)` —
one function, one parameter block, applied identically to every agent on every tick. That is the
right shape for the three canonical emergence demonstrations and it is the wrong shape for the
moment you want *this* agent to spend two seconds approaching, half a second feeding and then go
somewhere else. A global rule has no place to keep "where am I up to". You end up encoding the
agent's position in its own program as an integer state field and a `when`, which is the standard
way this is done and is also why it is never done twice the same way.

A coroutine has a place to keep it: the continuation. So a behaviour here reads as the sequence it
is —

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
forever {
    phase("travel") { moveUntil({ near(site, 6.0) }, maxSeconds = 8.0) { seek(site); separate() } }
    phase("feed")   { rest(0.4) }
}
```

— and the scheduler, not the author, remembers that this agent is 1.3 seconds into its approach.

### Why the scheduler counts ticks

The obvious way to build this is on `kotlinx.coroutines` with `delay` and a real dispatcher. That
gives you something you can watch and nothing you can assert, because the interleaving depends on
the machine. This scheduler is **mine and it counts ticks**:

 - `wait(seconds)` rounds **up** to a whole number of steps, `ceil(seconds / fixedStep)`, minimum
   one. Wake-ups are compared as `Long` tick numbers, so there is no floating-point boundary to be
   on the wrong side of, and `wait(0.5)` at 60 Hz is exactly 30 steps, every time.
 - Resumptions run from a FIFO queue I own, ordered by `(wakeTick, sequence)` with a unique
   monotonic sequence number, which is a **total** order. Two behaviours that wake on the same tick
   resume in the order they went to sleep.
 - Drives are held in a `LinkedHashMap` keyed by a monotonic `Long`, so they are evaluated in the
   order they were registered. (Keying a motor map by `Any()` — the natural thing, since the key is
   only a handle — makes the evaluation order depend on identity hash codes, i.e. on the run.)
 - Every drive reads a **pre-step snapshot** of every agent, so the result does not depend on which
   agent is integrated first.
 - Randomness is per agent, from `Random(seed, id)`, never from a shared stream, so adding an agent
   does not reshuffle the others.

The consequence is [`ScriptWorld.state`](alife.md#alife-script-kt--scriptworld--state): run a population twice from one seed and the `DoubleArray`
is equal bit for bit. That is asserted, not asserted-about — see `AlifeScriptGallery`.

### Composing, not duplicating

The steering verbs in [`BehaviourSteering`](alife.md#alife-script-kt-behavioursteering) are the Reynolds vocabulary already in this family:
[`BehaviourSteering.separate`](alife.md#alife-script-kt--behavioursteering--separate), [`BehaviourSteering.align`](alife.md#alife-script-kt--behavioursteering--align) and [`BehaviourSteering.cohere`](alife.md#alife-script-kt--behavioursteering--cohere) are the
three boid terms, so a scripted population can *be* a flock when its script says to be one, and
[`ScriptWorld.asBoidFlock`](alife.md#alife-script-kt--scriptworld--asboidflock) hands the state to [`polarization`](alife.md#alife-kt--polarization), [`nearestNeighborDistances`](alife.md#alife-kt--nearestneighbordistances) and the
rest of `alife.kt`'s measures rather than growing a second set. Trails come out as [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline)s
([`ScriptWorld.trailFLines`](alife.md#alife-script-kt--scriptworld--trailflines)) because geometry is FLine's job; nothing here rasterises anything
except where a contact sheet needs pixels.

### What it deliberately is not

Not a behaviour tree and not a blackboard. Both are ways of giving a *stateless* evaluator somewhere
to put the state, and the whole argument above is that a coroutine already has somewhere. There is
no reactive re-evaluation either: a behaviour that wants to abandon what it is doing says so, with
[`BehaviourScope.moveUntil`](alife.md#alife-script-kt--behaviourscope--moveuntil) or [`BehaviourScope.timeout`](alife.md#alife-script-kt--behaviourscope--timeout) or by cancelling a [`BehaviourJob`](alife.md#alife-script-kt-behaviourjob).

A fixed-step arena of scripted agents: the clock, the scheduler, the population and the physics.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <a id="alife-script-kt--scriptworld--width"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">width</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> |  |
| <a id="alife-script-kt--scriptworld--height"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">height</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> |  |
| <a id="alife-script-kt--scriptworld--fixedstep"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">fixedStep</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Seconds per tick. Also the quantum every [`BehaviourScope.wait`](alife.md#alife-script-kt--behaviourscope--wait) is rounded up to, so it sets the time resolution of every script in the world. |
| <a id="alife-script-kt--scriptworld--seed"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">seed</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span></code> |  |
| <a id="alife-script-kt--scriptworld--wrap"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">wrap</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code> | True for a torus (the metric [`BoidFlock`](alife.md#alife-agents-kt-boidflock) uses, and what `asBoidFlock` assumes); false to clamp at the walls, which stops agents but does not make them avoid them — that is [`BehaviourSteering.avoidEdges`](alife.md#alife-script-kt--behavioursteering--avoidedges)' job. |
| <a id="alife-script-kt--scriptworld--maxparallelperactor"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">maxParallelPerActor</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | The cap [`BehaviourScope.parallel`](alife.md#alife-script-kt--behaviourscope--parallel) checks. A behaviour that launches a sub-behaviour inside a `forever` and never cancels it is the standard way to fill a scheduler with garbage, and it presents as a gradual slowdown rather than an error. This turns it into an error. |
| <a id="alife-script-kt--scriptworld--maxresumptionsperstep"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">maxResumptionsPerStep</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | How many behaviour resumptions one step may take before the world declares a livelock. Catches the two shapes that otherwise hang: a `while (true)` with no `wait`, and a `wait` short enough to round to zero (it cannot — `wait` has a one-tick floor — but a hand-rolled `forever` over an empty body would still spin). |
| <a id="alife-script-kt--scriptworld--recordtrails"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">recordTrails</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code> | Whether to accumulate per-agent trails for [`trailFLines`](alife.md#alife-script-kt--scriptworld--trailflines). On by default because the trail is the picture; turn it off for long runs where only the final state matters. |
| <a id="alife-script-kt--scriptworld--maxroutesearchesperstep"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">maxRouteSearchesPerStep</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | How many [`BehaviourSteering.route`](alife.md#alife-script-kt--behavioursteering--route) drives may run a fresh A\* in one step. A grid search is the one thing in this file that is not `O(1)` per agent, and a population that all repaths on the same tick is the frame that drops. Agents over the budget keep steering to the route they already have and try again next step; the budget is spent in agent-id order, so which agents get it is reproducible. |
| <a id="alife-script-kt--scriptworld--maxrouteexpansions"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">maxRouteExpansions</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Cells one A\* may expand before giving up. A search that hits this returns no route rather than a bad one, and the drive falls back to a direct seek. |
| <a id="alife-script-kt--scriptworld--maxnavcells"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">maxNavCells</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | The cap on a [`NavGrid`](alife.md#alife-walls-kt-navgrid)'s cell count. Exceeding it enlarges the cells and sets [`NavGrid.coarse`](alife.md#alife-walls-kt--navgrid--coarse) rather than allocating a grid proportional to the arena. |

### ALifeBehaviour { #alife-script-kt-alifebehaviour }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">annotation</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">ALifeBehaviour</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/agents/alife_script/#L1270)

Marks the two scripting receivers, so a steering block cannot accidentally call a suspending behaviour verb on the enclosing scope.

## alife_trail.kt { #alife-trail-kt }

A stigmergy field on the GPU: a four-channel trail texture that agents write into and read from,
and that diffuses, decays and drifts on its own between their visits.

This is the medium of every "leave a mark, follow the marks" system: Physarum's chemoattractant,
ant pheromone, the dust in a particle system that remembers where the crowd went. [`TrailField`](alife.md#alife-trail-kt-trailfield)
owns only the medium. Whatever writes into it is a *deposit module* you add with [`addDeposit`](alife.md#alife-trail-kt--trailfield--adddeposit),
built on [`depositParameters`](alife.md#alife-trail-kt--trailfield--depositparameters); [`ShaderPhysarumSystem`](alife.md#alife-physarum-gpu-kt-shaderphysarumsystem) is one such writer, and its agent shader is
the worked example of reading the field back.

### One frame

The field is an RGBA16F [`PingPongRenderToTexture`](graphics.md#pingpongrendertotexture-kt-pingpongrendertotexture). Each frame, first, a full-screen *evolve* pass
rebuilds the field from the previous frame: it samples the old trail at `p - wind` (bilinear, so
sub-pixel wind drifts smoothly), mixes in the 3x3 mean by [`TrailFieldSettings.diffusion`](alife.md#alife-trail-kt--trailfieldsettings--diffusion), and
multiplies each channel by its decay. Then every deposit module draws, additively, into the same
target, reading the *previous* frame through `trailTex`. The four channels are independent trails
(four species, or one trail plus three other kinds of mark); each has its own half-life.

The field is toroidal: sampling and diffusion wrap at the edges.

### Reading it from a shader

`#include "trail/sample"` gives `trailAt(trailTex, px)` (bilinear, wrapping, pixel coordinates
with pixel centres at `+0.5`), `trailGradient(trailTex, px, weights, h)`, and `trailClip(px, dims)`
for placing a deposit point at a pixel. The same source is [`TrailShaders.SAMPLE`](alife.md#alife-trail-kt--trailshaders--sample) for code that
builds shader strings itself.

### Reading it from Kotlin

[`read`](alife.md#alife-trail-kt--trailfield--read) queues a copy of the raw floats and completes with an [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img) (four channels, unclamped);
`channel(c)` of that is what [`Img.topShare`](alife.md#alife-kt--topshare) takes.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/agents/alife_trail.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/agents/alife_trail/)

## alife_trail_followers.kt { #alife-trail-followers-kt }

Particles that steer by a [`TrailField`](alife.md#alife-trail-kt-trailfield): the reading half of stigmergy, for any particle system.

[`TrailFollowers`](alife.md#alife-trail-followers-kt-trailfollowers) keeps its particles (position and velocity, in trail pixels) in an addressable
buffer and moves them in one vertex-shader draw per frame. Each particle takes
`trailGradient(trailTex, p, weights, h)` from `#include "trail/sample"`, the gradient of
`dot(trail, weights)`, adds [`TrailFollowerSettings.steering`](alife.md#alife-trail-followers-kt--trailfollowersettings--steering) times its direction to its velocity,
damps, clamps to a top speed and steps, then draws itself as a point over the trail's preview. Positive weights climb a channel, negative ones flee it: weights `(1, -1, 0, 0)` ride
species 0's roads and keep out of species 1's.

The followers only read the field, so they can be added to a running [`ShaderPhysarumSystem`](alife.md#alife-physarum-gpu-kt-shaderphysarumsystem) (pass
its `trail`) or to any [`TrailField`](alife.md#alife-trail-kt-trailfield) another system writes. The rule is the host box's `vertex` tab,
unless that tab already holds another system's rule: build the followers in a box of their own
(beneath the one publishing the field) to edit theirs live.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/agents/alife_trail_followers.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/agents/alife_trail_followers/)

## alife_vehicle_brains.kt { #alife-vehicle-brains-kt }

A larger Braitenberg vehicle genome, and an equal-budget comparison of the searches that look for one.

[`VehicleWiringGenome`](alife.md#alife-evolve-kt-vehiclewiringgenome) is four numbers. A [`VehicleBrainGenome`](alife.md#alife-vehicle-brains-kt-vehiclebraingenome) adds what the vehicle model can
express besides its wires: where the sensors point, how sensitive they are, a bias on each motor,
and `VehicleBrainGenome.hidden` recurrent hidden neurons between the sensors and the motors. With no
hidden neurons it is 8 numbers; with 8 it is 112, with 16 it is 344. [`compareVehicleSearch`](alife.md#alife-vehicle-brains-kt--comparevehiclesearch) runs random sampling, a
hill climber and the (µ+λ) evolver of [`PopulationSearch`](search.md#populationsearch-kt-populationsearch) at the same evaluation budget over many
seeds and reports distributions, which is how `braitenberg_vehicles.md` §10 asks whether evolution
beats random sampling and at what genome size the answer changes.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/agents/alife_vehicle_brains.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/agents/alife_vehicle_brains/)

**Used in:** [Braitenberg vehicles with memory](../braitenberg_vehicles.md)

Random sampling, hill climbing and evolution on `task` with a `hidden`-neuron [`VehicleBrainGenome`](alife.md#alife-vehicle-brains-kt-vehiclebraingenome), each for exactly `budget` objective calls at every seed in `seeds`, through [`compareSearch`](search.md#searchcomparison-kt--comparesearch). Deterministic given its arguments. Evolution is (µ=`mu` + λ=`lambda`) with tournament 2, `crossoverRate` and `immigrantRate` (the fraction of children that are fresh random draws); the hill climber restarts after `patience` non-improving steps. For a fourth arm, or another genome, call [`compareSearch`](search.md#searchcomparison-kt--comparesearch) directly. |

## alife_walls.kt { #alife-walls-kt }

Walls for `alife_script.kt`: obstacles, swept circle collision, and radius-aware routing around
them.

See `alife_script.kt` for the scripting layer this completes, and `alife.kt` for the family
overview.

### Why this exists

[`ScriptWorld`](alife.md#alife-script-kt-scriptworld) shipped as a bare rectangle. The only spatial thing an agent could say was
[`BehaviourSteering.avoidEdges`](alife.md#alife-script-kt--behavioursteering--avoidedges), which pushes away from the four sides of the arena; everything
else a scripted agent could steer around was another agent. That rules out the whole category of
behaviour that is *about* the environment — a corridor, a room with a door, a barrier you have to
go round rather than through — and it rules it out silently, because an agent pressing into a
wall that does not exist just flies on.

### Three representations

**Obstacles are a flat soup of line segments** ([`ScriptObstacle`](alife.md#alife-walls-kt-scriptobstacle), [`ObstacleField`](alife.md#alife-walls-kt-obstaclefield)) and not
polygons-as-solids. The only predicate collision needs is "is this swept circle crossing a wall",
which a segment answers directly; making obstacles *solid* would mean a point-in-polygon test, a
winding rule, and an answer for what two overlapping solids mean. A soup accepts an open wall, a
concave room, a fence with a gap in it and two shapes that cross, all without a special case. The
price is stated rather than hidden: there is no "inside", so nothing stops an agent that *starts*
inside a closed shape from staying there — [`ScriptWorld.spawn`](alife.md#alife-script-kt--scriptworld--spawn) pushes it out to the nearest
surface instead of teleporting it somewhere arbitrary.

**Collision is swept**, not discrete ([`ObstacleField.sweep`](alife.md#alife-walls-kt--obstaclefield--sweep)). A discrete test asks whether the
agent's new position overlaps a wall, which is false for any agent whose per-step displacement is
larger than the wall is thick — and a wall here is a segment, so it is *infinitely* thin and a
discrete test can miss it at any speed at all. The swept test solves for the first fraction of the
step at which the moving circle touches, so a projectile at 600 units/s stops at the wall it would
otherwise have crossed in one tick. `AlifeWallsGallery`'s tunnelling figure runs both.

**Navigation is a uniform occupancy grid inflated by the agent's radius, searched with A\*, then
string-pulled against the exact segment test** ([`NavGrid`](alife.md#alife-walls-kt-navgrid)). The obvious alternative is a
visibility graph, which is exact and gives shorter paths from a much smaller search. It was
rejected on *construction*, not on search: a visibility graph over a segment soup needs its
corners offset outward by the agent radius, and "the offset corner" is not defined where two
segments cross, nearly touch, or are collinear — which is precisely the geometry that appears
when a user draws a wall twice or butts two rectangles together. A grid has no corners to reason
about: it is built by one distance query per cell per segment, radius-awareness is a single
inflation number, and the one thing it gets wrong — paths that staircase along cell centres — is
removed afterwards by [`NavGrid.stringPull`](alife.md#alife-walls-kt--navgrid--stringpull), which uses the same exact swept test the physics does.
A coarse grid can still *over*-block a narrow gap; [`NavGrid.coarse`](alife.md#alife-walls-kt--navgrid--coarse) says when that happened rather
than leaving the caller to wonder why there was no route.

### Determinism

The same property the rest of `alife_script.kt` depends on, and the same discipline. Segments
are held in insertion order in flat `DoubleArray`s. A*'s open set is ordered by `(f, cellIndex)`,
a **total** order, so two cells with equal estimated cost expand in a fixed order rather than in
whichever order a heap happened to leave them. Neighbours are visited through one fixed
eight-element offset table. The nav-grid cache is a `LinkedHashMap` keyed by the quantised
inflation radius. The per-step route budget is consumed in agent-id order, because drives are
evaluated in agent-id order. Nothing here reads a clock or a hash set.

## alife_ca.kt { #alife-ca-kt }

Discrete cellular automata: life-like and outer-totalistic rules on a 2-D lattice, cyclic
multi-state CA, Wolfram's elementary 1-D rules as a space-time raster, and a 3-D life-like CA that
marches out to a [`TriMesh`](graphics.md#mesh-kt-trimesh).

See `alife.kt` for the family overview and for [`IntGrid`](alife.md#alife-kt-intgrid), the lattice everything here steps.

The design commitment worth stating: a *rule* is a value ([`LifeRule`](alife.md#alife-ca-kt-liferule)), separate from the grid it is
applied to. That is what lets the gallery run the same glider under `B3/S23` and under a
deliberately-wrong neighbour rule and show that only one of them translates — and what lets
`alife_continuous.kt`'s Lenia stepper be checked against this file's discrete stepper in the limit
where the two must agree.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/automata/alife_ca.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/automata/alife_ca/)

**Used in:** [Spatial artificial life](../alife_examples.md), [Three-dimensional Life, counted and traced](../chain_life3d_render.md)

### LifeRule { #alife-ca-kt-liferule }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">LifeRule</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">birth</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Set</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">survive</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Set</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">radius</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">vonNeumann</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">false</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">notation</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s">&quot;B${birth.sorted().joinToString(&quot;</span><span class="s">&quot;)}/S${survive.sorted().joinToString(&quot;</span><span class="s">&quot;)}&quot;</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/automata/alife_ca/#L108)

An outer-totalistic two-state rule: a cell's next state depends only on its own state and on **how many** of its neighbours are alive, not on which.

| <a id="alife-ca-kt--liferule--survive"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">survive</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Set</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | Neighbour counts at which a live cell stays alive. |

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">CyclicRule</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">states</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">threshold</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">radius</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">vonNeumann</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">false</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/automata/alife_ca/#L445)

### LifeRule3D { #alife-ca-kt-liferule3d }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">LifeRule3D</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">birth</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Set</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">survive</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Set</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/automata/alife_ca/#L753)

A 3-D outer-totalistic rule over the 26-voxel Moore neighbourhood — the direct generalisation of [`LifeRule`](alife.md#alife-ca-kt-liferule). Notation is the same `B…/S…`, with counts up to 26, so `B5/S45` is written `LifeRule3D(setOf(5), setOf(4, 5))`.
